status: Design-stage literature assessment; no Assignment 10 numerical outcomes inspected.
primary_source_policy: Substantive claims rely on original articles, author manuscripts or primary publisher/institution records. Access and version limits are explicit; no finding that no identical study exists is proof of novelty.
research_standard: Candid significance; explicit problem, reason it matters, nearest results, exact supported increment and limitations; standard defined terminology for a mature nonspecialist; no inflated novelty, generality or publication prospects. Finance/econometrics does not use the mathematics production workflow.

comparison_table.citation: Bollen and Pool (2009), Do Hedge Fund Managers Misreport Returns? Evidence from the Pooled Distribution, Journal of Finance 64(5), 2257–2288.
comparison_table.version: Published article; 2007 SSRN version is earlier, not interchangeable.
comparison_table.inspection: Publisher abstract and article metadata inspected; published PDF request returned 403.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Documents a pooled monthly-return discontinuity near zero, absent around audits and disappearing in two-month returns; interprets this as evidence consistent with temporary overstatement.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Loss deferral and return patterns near zero are established subjects.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Compare declared screening choices at common warning budgets, with economically reconciled temporary recognition and genuinely separate validation.
comparison_table.limits: Our fitted-normal negative-month count is not their pooled local density test. The paper does not establish that every individual kink proves fraud.

comparison_table.citation: Bollen and Pool (2008), Conditional Return Smoothing in the Hedge Fund Industry, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 43(2), 267–298.
comparison_table.version: Published metadata plus January 2006 author precursor, A screen for fraudulent return smoothing in the hedge fund industry.
comparison_table.inspection: Publisher page and precursor introduction/model motivation and error/power discussion inspected through primary-site web text; old PDF URL currently 404 for local download.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Models fully reporting gains while delaying losses; conditional serial correlation can screen this behavior. The precursor already studies false alarms, missed deferral, record length and scarce audit resources.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Mechanism-based power and prioritizing investigations are not new.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Show whether competing declared screens or combinations transfer across reporting mechanisms and strategy/date groups.
comparison_table.limits: Conditional serial correlation differs from simple lag 1 ACF; the precursor simulates risk-factor returns and distinguishes known from inferred exposures. Do not attribute precursor numerical rates to final 2008 without checking.

comparison_table.citation: Bollen and Pool (2012), Suspicious Patterns in Hedge Fund Returns and the Risk of Fraud, Review of Financial Studies 25(9), 2673–2702.
comparison_table.version: Published article and November 21, 2011 author-version bibliographic record.
comparison_table.inspection: Primary author abstract inspected. Published Table 8 definition and warning-budget structure checked in indexed original-paper excerpt; publisher/SSRN full PDFs denied, so exact regression specifications not verified.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Combines suspicious-return flags in probit violation probabilities; an f-score divides conditional by unconditional violation probability. Table 8 compares reporting/trading violation detection at thresholds corresponding to 5%/10% comparison-fund warnings.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: The closest direct prior work already joins return flags and compares detection against warning frequency.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Provide a reproducible controlled reporting-mechanism comparison and credible transfer evidence, rather than claim to invent a combined return screen.
comparison_table.limits: Violations are observed enforcement/legal outcomes, not a complete set of all frauds; comparison funds are not certified honest. Exact published coefficients were not retrieved and must not be claimed replicated.

comparison_table.citation: Abdulali (2006), The Bias Ratio: Measuring the Shape of Fraud, Protégé Partners Quarterly Letter, Q 3.
comparison_table.version: Original quarterly letter not retrieved; same-inventor patent with 2006 priority inspected separately.
comparison_table.inspection: Original URL timed out. Patent description inspected as a primary account of the statistic, not as a substitute for the letter.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: The inventor patent defines a near-zero positive/negative histogram-count ratio, comparison benchmarks and flags.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: The score and benchmark idea are existing practitioner work.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Measure how useful the declared bias score is relative to other families across specific held-out economic settings.
comparison_table.limits: Do not attribute a universally validated cutoff 2, or exact original-letter empirical results, to Abdulali without the original. Patent is not peer-reviewed validation.

comparison_table.citation: Jorion and Schwarz (2014), Are Hedge Fund Managers Systematically Misreporting? Or Not?, Journal of Financial Economics 111(2), 311–327.
comparison_table.version: Published abstract and publisher-indexed substantive text; earlier SSRN revision 2013.
comparison_table.inspection: Publisher abstract and indexed sections on fees and pooled return distributions inspected; direct full-text requests 403.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Shows incentive fees can mechanically produce a zero-return kink, substantially explaining that pattern in liquid long–short equity; illiquidity and bounded yields provide further alternatives.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: A warning need not identify manipulation; return definition and legitimate economics already matter.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Quantify the declared rules under explicit gross/spread/funded conventions and distinguish practical investigation triggers from attribution.
comparison_table.limits: Does not show that all reporting distortions are unidentifiable or every screen is useless.

comparison_table.citation: Joshua van Vuuren and Gary van Vuuren (2022), Detecting Investment Fraud Using the Bias Ratio, SAGE Open 12(2).
comparison_table.inspection: Publisher full article text inspected, including index data, return-moment comparisons, known cases and limitations; PDF 403.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Applies bias ratios with statistical moments to strategy indices and known fraud cases; discusses good performance and illiquidity as reasons to investigate carefully.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Bias-plus-moments interpretation and high-performance caution are already present.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: A common-budget, held-out comparison with imposed mechanisms would be more disciplined than illustrative cases, if it yields stable and useful differences.
comparison_table.limits: Strategy-index analysis and retrospective cases do not establish a validated universal classifier.

comparison_table.citation: Joenväärä and Kosowski (2015), Effect of Regulatory Constraints on Fund Performance: New Evidence from UCITS Hedge Funds, working paper/CEPRDP 10577.
comparison_table.version: September 15, 2015 author paper downloaded; CEPR entry revised 2019, which was not treated as this same version.
comparison_table.inspection: Introduction, suspicious-return section, Table 3, operational-risk comparison and AppendixB.2.1 inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Uses existing return diagnostics, mentions their sum and reports a first-principal-component measure; UCITS have fewer suspicious return patterns while operational-risk measures need not be lower.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: UCITS screening comparisons and score aggregation already exist.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Test frozen combinations for transfer, rather than equate a regulated wrapper with verified honesty.
comparison_table.limits: The paper mostly uses test statistics instead of indicators. It gives suspicion directions but no explicit PCA normalization/loadings/sign formula, so standardized train-only PCA is an inspired comparator, not exact replication.

comparison_table.citation: Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004), An Econometric Model of Serial Correlation and Illiquidity in Hedge Fund Returns, Journal of Financial Economics 74, 529–609.
comparison_table.version: Published article downloaded from coauthor institution.
comparison_table.inspection: Abstract, economic explanation and smoothing-model sections inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Develops a lagged-return smoothing model, smoothing-adjusted Sharpe ratios and evidence varying by hedge-fund style. Illiquidity and discretionary marking can generate dependence.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: ACF and moving-average smoothing are established diagnostics/mechanisms.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Separate what a screen detects under declared filters from what can be attributed to deliberate manipulation.
comparison_table.limits: A positive ACF is not a fraud label, and liquid reconstructed stock portfolios do not represent all valuation processes.

comparison_table.citation: Cassar and Gerakos (2011), Hedge Funds: Pricing Controls and the Smoothing of Self-reported Returns, Review of Financial Studies 24(5), 1698–1734.
comparison_table.version: Published abstract; old author PDF URL now 404.
comparison_table.inspection: Publisher abstract and indexed first page inspected; full PDF not retrieved.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Uses observed pricing processes to distinguish asset-illiquidity explanations from greater managerial discretion; investment style/holdings characteristics explain more smoothing variation than pricing controls.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: The distinction between a return symptom and its economic cause is already central.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Our controlled alterations can map symptoms to known imposed mechanisms, but cannot identify those mechanisms in Fund X without external information.
comparison_table.limits: The additional valuation evidence in this paper is richer than our return-only data.

comparison_table.citation: Dimmock and Gerken (2012), Predicting Fraud by Investment Managers, Journal of Financial Economics 105(1), 153–173.
comparison_table.version: Published abstract plus March 1, 2011 author version downloaded.
comparison_table.inspection: Published abstract; precursor prediction, false-positive-budget, temporal holdout and cross-validation sections inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Predicts subsequent fraud using mandatory disclosures; published abstract reports that avoiding the riskiest 5% of firms would avoid 29% of fraud cases and over 40% of dollar losses. Precursor explicitly evaluates fixed false-warning budgets and out-of-sample predictions.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Prioritization, cost implications and validation are established, although using non-return information.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Show the incremental decisions supportable by returns alone, recognizing that we lack their fraud outcomes and disclosure data.
comparison_table.limits: Do not transfer their real-loss benefits to our imposed reporting alterations or call chronological validation alone novel.

comparison_table.citation: Beneish and Vorst (2022), The Cost of Fraud Prediction Errors, The Accounting Review 97(6), 91–121.
comparison_table.version: Accepted author manuscript downloaded from author institution.
comparison_table.inspection: Abstract, introduction, model-comparison metrics and auditor/investor/regulator cost sections inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Compares seven fraud models by net benefits, error costs and limited investigation capacity. Better detection can be economically unattractive because false warnings are numerous; conclusions differ by decision maker.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: A detection/false-warning frontier or cost tradeoff is not a new method.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Offer new fund-return evidence at stated budgets and show how conclusions change across reporting mechanisms; use cost/prevalence scenarios when actual costs are unknown.
comparison_table.limits: Corporate financial-statement setting and observed misconduct differ from our reconstructed portfolios. Our data cannot estimate real fraud prevalence or monetary losses avoided.

comparison_table.citation: Bao, Ke, Li, Yu and Zhang (2020), Detecting Accounting Fraud in Publicly Traded U.S. Firms Using a Machine Learning Approach, Journal of Accounting Research 58(1), 199–235; Erratum(2022), 60(4), 1635–1646.
comparison_table.version: Published article abstract and full 2022 correction.
comparison_table.inspection: Publisher abstract and correction sections 1–3, including corrected top-k and AUC comparisons, inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: An ensemble fraud model is compared with alternatives; the correction documents how fraud firms spanning training and test can inflate performance and changes some top-k comparisons.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Score ensembles, chronological evaluation and ranking within small investigation budgets are established.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Keep strategy identities and all altered versions together in strategy validation; assess low-budget detection rather than rely only on overall AUC.
comparison_table.limits: Accounting inputs and observed fraud labels differ from returns. Cite corrected results; do not claim all model advantages disappeared.

comparison_table.citation: González, Papageorgiou and Skinner (2016), Persistent Doubt: An Examination of Hedge Fund Performance, European Financial Management 22(4), 613–639.
comparison_table.inspection: Publisher introduction, performance-sorted portfolio methods, strategy results, later-period comparisons and diagnostic interpretation inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Studies top-quintile funds chosen by Sharpe and other performance measures, subsequent persistence and the doubt ratio. It acknowledges legitimate carry/arbitrage can produce suspicious-looking histories.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Selection among strong performers, strategy stratification and later diagnostic behavior are not new topics.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Show different operating tradeoffs for the declared tests and specified reporting policies under credible validation and adequate high-performance support.
comparison_table.limits: A doubt ratio is not proof of misconduct; our four chosen families do not exhaust return-only diagnostics.

comparison_table.citation: Bailey and López de Prado (2014), The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality, Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5), 94–107.
comparison_table.inspection: Abstract, winner-selection argument and deflated-Sharpe construction inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Adjusts performance inference for searching across candidate strategies and non-normal return distributions.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Selection and skewness-aware performance inference are established.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Our object is reporting-screen behavior after selection, which differs from testing investment skill, and that distinction must be explicit.
comparison_table.limits: DSR is not a fraud detector and cannot supply fraud labels or authenticate Fund X.

comparison_table.citation: Davis and Goadrich (2006), The Relationship Between Precision-Recall and ROC Curves, ICML, 233–240.
comparison_table.inspection: Introduction, definitions and dominance/interpolation results inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Detection/false-positive curves and precision-recall comparisons are established tools; rare-class prevalence matters for the practical interpretation of warnings.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: A frontier itself is standard classifier evaluation.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Report declared operating budgets, detection and warning burden; make any precision/net-benefit calculation explicitly conditional on assumed prevalence.
comparison_table.limits: Our paired baseline/altered dataset artificially determines class frequency; its apparent precision is not real-world fraud precision.

comparison_table.citation: Chowdhry and Saxena (2026), Detecting Lies When Truth is Unobservable, working paper, SSRN 6445461.
comparison_table.version: March 18 author PDF 39-pages downloaded; SSRN entry last revised July 29 is 111-pages and is a different version.
comparison_table.inspection: March introduction, assumptions, Section 5.10 skewness sensitivity and conclusion inspected; July abstract only.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Proposes downside-variation diagnostics for one-sided reporting. March version shows symmetry is needed for its simple null and skewness can cause false warnings; July abstract adds Madoff/Berkshire and earnings examples.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Distribution-sensitive reporting diagnostics and their identification limits have current direct overlap.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: A cross-mechanism comparison on observed strategy returns could add evidence, but must not claim the four existing families exhaust methods.
comparison_table.limits: Not peer-reviewed. Do not criticize July revision as simulation-only based on March PDF or treat author claims as verified theorems.

comparison_table.citation: Boudt, Delmarcelle and Ringoot (2025), A News Monitoring System to Detect Relevant News for the Anti-Money Laundering Supervision of Financial Institutions, Risk Sciences 1, 100018.
comparison_table.version: Published open-access PDF downloaded from author institution.
comparison_table.inspection: Introduction, analyst workflow, score/threshold construction, event analysis, robustness and conclusion inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Builds a news-alert system tied to supervisory workflow, demonstrates relevance around eight offshore leaks and examines translation/other robustness.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Venue example of a clear applied risk decision and supporting evidence.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Explain who investigates, what fixed warning budget means and what additional reconciliation a warning should trigger.
comparison_table.limits: Alerts identify relevant news, not established wrongdoing. One venue example does not set a universal acceptance threshold.

comparison_table.citation: Eling and Jung (2025 issue; online 2024), Optimism Bias and Its Impact on Cyber Risk Management Decisions, Risk Sciences 1, 100001.
comparison_table.version: Publisher-listed 2025 article; early published PDF displays 2024.
comparison_table.inspection: Published abstract, model framing and conclusion inspected.
comparison_table.what_previous_work_shows: Models how reference points and loss aversion change choices among self-protection, insurance and other risk controls.
comparison_table.overlap_with_proposed_study: Venue example ties a specified economic mechanism to an identifiable decision.
comparison_table.what_we_would_have_to_add: Connect screen performance to a concrete investor choice and quantify where that choice changes.
comparison_table.limits: Different subject and theoretical design; not evidence that our empirical extension meets the research-article contribution requirement.

novelty_assessment.verdict: A useful empirical validation extension is possible; a substantial advance is not established by the design alone.
already_standard: Combining diagnostic scores by OR, counts, averages, PCA or learned models
Using warnings to prioritize limited investigations
Caution about selection, skewness and innocent economic explanations
novelty_assessment.potential_supported_increment: A transparent, reproducible comparison of specified fund-return screens and fixed combinations that demonstrates whether a choice learned from earlier strategies and reporting mechanisms survives new dates, new strategy groups and different reporting mechanisms, particularly where performance is genuinely high.
must_show: Economically material held-out differences at the same investigation or baseline-warning budget, compared with strong predeclared single-score and aggregation benchmarks.
Whether the rule survives strategy separation as well as calendar separation, with same-strategy altered versions kept together and shared shocks respected.
Whether good detection of one policy transfers to another, rather than merely recognizing the transformation used in training.
Adequate observed support for the declared high-performance subgroup, with its financial return convention and costs clear.
A concrete investigation decision that changes, plus its missed-problem cost; threshold selection must precede final evaluation.
novelty_assessment.if_results_disappoint: Report that the declared rules have mechanism-dependent strengths or fail to transfer. This is evidence about these rules and scenarios, not a universal impossibility result.
not_supported: A new statistical frontier or ensemble method merely from combining the four families.
Verified false-positive rates among honest managers, real fraud classification, actual fraud prevalence or actual monetary losses avoided.
Authentication of Fund X, proof of misconduct, or an explanation of its performance from unmatched factor histories.
An exhaustive evaluation of all return-based methods, or a first-ever claim without a fuller review.

methodological_implications: Separate a frozen implementable rule from an envelope chosen after observing final test results; the latter is exploratory.
Report baseline warnings and imposed-policy detection as separate quantities. Artificial 50/50 pairing cannot estimate real precision.
For investigation costs, use stated prevalence/cost scenarios or break-even ratios; do not estimate unknown fraud prevalence from reconstructed portfolios.
Describe the fitted-normal count as the paper adaptation, not the original pooled Bollen–Pool local test.
SimpleACF does not replicate conditional serial correlation; state the chosen four-family scope.
Use all-strategy and high-performance analyses separately; a high ratio created by cash interest or rescaling is not matched economic performance.
If a method fails to reject an altered record, that establishes a miss under this policy, not a general immunity to fraud detection.

risk_sciences.verified_scope: General-interest risk research and industry practice includes finance, statistics and risk governance; welcomes research, industrial case studies and perspectives.
risk_sciences.verified_research_article_standard: Guide describes research articles as original reports of substantial advances concerning an important scientific problem.
risk_sciences.implication: Subject is within scope. A careful applied empirical paper needs a precise practical contribution beyond familiar diagnostic caveats; the examples do not establish that this study is sufficient or imply acceptance prospects.

access_gaps: Bollen–Pool 2009/2012 full primary PDFs not retrieved locally; exact 2012 regression coefficients not claimed verified.
Jorion–Schwarz 2014 full PDF not retrieved; assessment uses published abstract and indexed publisher text.
Joenväärä–Kosowski 2015 PDF is an author version;2019 revision not inspected.
Chowdhry–Saxena latest 111-page revision not retrieved; author 39-pageMarch version and latest abstract clearly distinguished.
